newsitem.title: INDIA: Reviled Hindu volunteers help India crash rescue.
newsitem.headline: Reviled Hindu volunteers help India crash rescue.

text.p: Wearing a cloth mask to keep out the stench of rotting flesh and the saffron headband of his much reviled Hindu Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), Rajesh Jangi hauled a piece of human limb into a truck.

"This is a gut-wrenching tragedy," he told Reuters on a still dark and cold Wednesday morning, hours after a Saudi jumbo jet and a Kazhakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided in the sky near Delhi, killing all 349 passengers and crew.
"All the volunteers helping out here belong to the RSS (National Volunteer Corps)," Jangi said.
"We could not save any lives, but we are doing the only thing we possibly could for the dead. That's what are are trained to do in any calamity."

Many of the 312 victims aboard the Saudi jumbo jet were Indian workers, mostly Moslems, some on a pilgrimage to Saudi Arabia. The Kazakh freighter was carrying 37 people. There were some Christians among the dead as well. The crash, on Tuesday, was the world's worst mid-air collision.
"It doesn't matter who these people are. They are human beings," said Jeet Ram Gupta, district president of the RSS in Charkhi Dadri, 80 kilometres (50 miles) west of Delhi.

"RSS volunteers were the first to reach the crash site and they would be the last to leave," Gupta told Reuters at the Charkhi Dadri hospital, as his colleagues unloaded the mangled and charred bodies they had brought in on tractor-trolleys.
At the site of the crash wreckage in Kheri Sanwal village, six kilometres (four miles) away, RSS volunteers picked up the bodies with bare hands from the smouldering debris.
"I thank (the volunteers). Allah will bless them," said Jumman Shah, a relative of a Moslem victim as he watched RSS workers unload slabs of ice and white cloth to preserve and cover the bodies.

Shunned by most Indian political parties as a Hindu bigot group for its perceived bias against the country's Moslems and Christians, the RSS was set up in the 1920s in the central Indian city of Nagpur.

Its leaders have been jailed and the party was banned on several occasions begining with the assassination of Indian nationalist leader Mahatma Gandhi in 1948, when the RSS was accused of backing his killer.
RSS workers first gained official acceptance in 1965, when they were assigned the task of civil defence in New Delhi during India's second war with Pakistan.

Banned again in 1975 for their opposition to then prime minister Indira Gandhi's emergency rule, the RSS attracted national critcism in 1992 when its leaders were accused of leading the demolition of a 16th century mosque in Ayodhya.
Then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao sacked all of the four state governments headed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the political arm of the RSS, over the mosque's destruction.
But the BJP, undeterred by Rao's hostility, emerged as the largest single group from this year's general election, leaving Rao's Congress party a poor second and suffering its worst poll defeat.
The BJP formed a government for 14 days but was forced to resign when no major political party was willing to support it.
The RSS, ignoring traditional hostility towards it from India's mainstream secular parties, has continued to woo more and more young volunteers.

RSS officials said its volunteers were active in this month's cyclone calamity in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh where they were helping with rehabilitation. The death toll from the cyclone ran into the hundreds.

"This is not the first time we are doing this kind of thing," district president Gupta said. "Our men were perhaps the only people lifting rotting bodies when a cyclone struck Andhra Pradesh in 1977."
More than 10,000 people were killed in that cyclone.
